paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould had killed bacteria on one of his dishes, he began a revolution in medicine. Antibiotics transformed infections that had been deadly, such as pneumonia and blood poisoning, into treatable conditions, and made modern surgery and cancer treatment possible. Yet Fleming himself warned, in his Nobel Prize speech in 1945, that careless use of penicillin could teach microbes to resist it. His warning has proved prophetic.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Resistance arises through natural selection. In any large population of bacteria, a few may carry a mutation that protects them from a particular drug. When an antibiotic kills the susceptible majority, the resistant minority survives and multiplies, and its descendants inherit the protection. Bacteria can also pass resistance genes directly to other bacteria, even to different species, which speeds up the process considerably. The more often antibiotics are used, the more opportunities this selection has.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Overuse has been widespread. Studies suggest that around a third of antibiotic prescriptions in some countries are unnecessary, often given for viral infections such as colds, against which antibiotics are useless. Farming is another major source: in many parts of the world, more antibiotics are given to healthy livestock to promote growth and prevent disease than to people. Patients also contribute by stopping treatment early, which can leave the hardiest bacteria alive.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The consequences are serious. The World Health Organization estimates that drug-resistant infections contribute to over a million deaths each year, and warns that without action, they could become one of the leading causes of death by 2050. Routine operations such as hip replacements could become dangerous if infections could not be controlled. The problem is made worse by an economic reality: since antibiotics are taken for short periods, they are less profitable than drugs for chronic conditions, and few companies invest in developing new ones.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Solutions exist, though none is simple. Doctors can prescribe more carefully and use rapid tests to identify whether an infection is bacterial. Governments can restrict antibiotic use in farming, as the European Union has done for growth promotion. Researchers are exploring alternatives, including bacteriophages, viruses that attack bacteria, and attempts to harness artificial intelligence to discover new molecules. Meanwhile, public understanding matters: antibiotics are a shared resource, and each unnecessary use diminishes it for everyone.
